comparison: Perfect agreement on dataset and analytical approach (C2, C34, C38-C40, C144). Both evaluations explicitly acknowledge the comprehensive scale (~17,000 transcriptomes, 35 tissues) and sophisticated analytical methods. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Perfect agreement on AMG expression patterns (C137-C141). Both evaluations support the clustering analysis, sex-specific temporal patterns, and functional enrichment findings. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these detailed characterizations as part of the comprehensive analysis they praise.

Strong agreement on study limitations and mitigation strategies (C166, C171-C178). OpenEval explicitly evaluates the authors' honest assessment of limitations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept these through positive assessment of methodological rigor and lack of major concerns about confounding factors.

Strong agreement on methodological validation and quality controls (C67-C76). OpenEval details specific validation analyses. Peer Reviewer 2 explicitly acknowledges consideration of 'important variables such as genetic background, ethnicity, sampling bias, sample sizes.' Both evaluations support the analytical rigor.

Agreement on estrogen-mediated regulation of female-specific SFs (C5, C100-C119, C185-C186). Both evaluations support the ChIP-Atlas analysis and experimental validation. OpenEval notes the mechanistic link is correlative; peer reviewers acknowledge this as a key conclusion without challenging the evidence.

Agreement on sex-dimorphic aging rates and breakpoint analysis (C6, C36, C121-C125, C147, C187). Both evaluations support the finding of earlier and larger transcriptome changes in males. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly calls this 'an important finding.' Both accept the ARIMA-based breakpoint methodology.

Agreement on high-level summary findings (C3, C48-C50, C59, C66, C82, C145). Both evaluations support widespread sex-dimorphic changes in gene expression and alternative splicing. Peer Reviewer 2 notes this is 'likely the first study' at this scale. Both recognize the comprehensive multi-level analyses.

Agreement on male-biased AS-AD associations (C4, C35, C83-C84, C86, C91-C92, C97). Both evaluations support the overlap analysis with AD datasets and validation in ROSMAP. Peer Reviewer 3 explicitly acknowledges this as a key conclusion. Peer Reviewer 1 calls it 'an important finding.'

Agreement on AMG identification and functional characterization (C126-C136, C162-C163, C192). Both evaluations support the disturbance analysis approach and functional enrichment patterns. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through overall positive assessment of the comprehensive aging analysis.

Agreement on differential overlap patterns between GE and AS (C78-C82, C120). Both evaluations support the hypergeometric tests and inference about stronger sex dimorphism in AS. Peer reviewers acknowledge the study identified both GE and AS changes with differential patterns.

Partial agreement on pcSVR analysis findings (C45-C59). OpenEval provides detailed evaluation of statistical tests and tissue-specific patterns. Peer reviewers acknowledge tissue-specific patterns and consideration of important variables, though less explicitly focused on pcSVR methodology.

Agreement on differential expression/splicing analysis methodology (C60-C66). OpenEval details the linear regression models and control analyses. Peer reviewers acknowledge sophisticated modeling and consideration of confounding variables, supporting the methodological approach.

Agreement on specific AS events associated with AD pathology (C93-C96). Both evaluations support the sex-specific associations with plaques/tangles and prediction model performance. Peer reviewers accept these as supporting evidence for broader male-biased AS-AD associations.

Agreement on SF regulatory network analysis (C5, C100-C105). OpenEval details the multi-step network construction. Peer reviewers acknowledge this as part of the comprehensive analysis showing estrogen receptor regulation of female-biased AS events.

Agreement on hormone receptor binding to AMGs (C133-C136, C162-C163, C192). Both evaluations support the ChIP-Atlas findings. OpenEval notes the mechanistic interpretation requires additional validation; peer reviewers accept as part of the comprehensive hormone-aging analysis.

Agreement on key abstract findings including male-biased AD-AS association (C4-C7, C35-C36). Both evaluations support these high-level conclusions. Peer reviewers explicitly acknowledge male-biased AS-AD associations and earlier male transcriptome changes.

Agreement on temporal correspondence with hormone decline (C7, C189-C190). Both evaluations support the finding that transcriptome changes coincide with sex hormone decline timing. Peer Reviewer 1 explicitly calls this 'an important finding.'

Agreement on mechanistic role of sex hormones (C7, C184-C190). Both evaluations support the temporal correlation between breakpoints and hormone decline. Peer reviewers note 'sex dimorphic shifts begin with declining sex hormone levels.'

Agreement on hormone decline timing and connection to aging (C189-C190, C7). Both evaluations support the established knowledge of hormone decline timing and its correspondence with observed breakpoints. Peer reviewers accept this temporal correlation.

Agreement on mitigation strategies for study limitations (C175-C176, C179, C182-C183). OpenEval explicitly evaluates the methodological approaches to address limitations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept through positive assessment of analytical rigor.

Partial overlap on AD associations (C89). OpenEval focuses on male-biased AS-AD associations. Peer R11 acknowledges complementary female GE-AD findings. Both support sex-dimorphic AD vulnerabilities from different molecular perspectives.

Partial overlap on ROSMAP validation (C91, C157-C158). OpenEval evaluates ROSMAP validation of AD-AS associations. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this validation as strengthening the findings, noting the comprehensive nature of the analysis.
